short.headline: India's electricity demand peaks in the evening, not when the sun is out.
short.dek: Solar pushes down midday net demand by about 22%, but after sunset the real peak hits around 7pm, driving a 40 GW ramp in six hours.
short.body: On an average summer day, India's grid sees demand hover around 210 GW through the late morning, while solar generation surges to about 48 GW at midday. Subtract solar and net demand sags to a belly of about 161 GW by 1pm. Then the sun sets and demand climbs to roughly 202 GW around 7pm. The evening ramp is the grid's hardest hour, and annual peaks keep rising, from about 159 GW in 2017 to a record 249 GW in 2024, a 57% jump. More panels won't solve a clock problem; storage and flexible power must fill the gap.

macha.heading: Okay, macha, so the sun is fooling us?
macha.body: The grid's biggest headache isn't just about how much power India needs—it's about when. Solar gives us a huge midday boost, but exactly when we all switch on lights and ACs after sunset, solar drops to zero. So every evening, the grid has to scramble to cover a sharp jump in demand, and that jump keeps getting bigger each year. Think of it like a family dinner: the sun cooks a big meal at noon, but everyone is actually hungry at 7pm, and by then the kitchen is cold. India doesn't just need more power; it needs power that shows up at the right hour.
macha.soWhat: The real power struggle is not about how much, but when.

article.title: When Does India Actually Turn the Power On?
article.standfirst: India's electricity demand peaks after dark, while solar generation vanishes. The evening ramp now dictates the grid's hardest hour, and that hour keeps climbing.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## When does India actually use the most electricity?

Not when you might think, and not when the sun is blazing. On an average summer day the grid is already working hard by late morning: total demand hovers around 210 GW through the late morning and afternoon. Right about then, solar comes flooding in. At its peak around midday, solar pushes out about 48 GW, covering roughly a fifth of everything the country is drawing. If you strip that solar out and look at what the rest of the system has to supply, the line sags through the middle of the afternoon into a distinct belly, net demand drops to about 161 GW at 1pm.

Then the sun goes down. Solar generation collapses toward zero. People come home, lights and fans and ACs stay on, and demand climbs to its real high for the day around seven in the evening, touching about 202 GW. That is a steep ramp: roughly 40 GW added in about six hours. And from 1pm to 7pm, solar’s share of demand falls from about 22% to essentially nothing. No amount of midday sunshine can cover an evening that arrives after sunset. The shape of that net-demand line, low belly, sharp evening neck, is the duck curve, and it captures the core timing mismatch that now defines India’s grid challenge.

## Does the peak hour change across the year?

The daily shape is not locked to one clock. As seasons turn, the curve shifts. In summer and the monsoon, demand stays high from late morning well into the evening, riding a broad plateau. Winter tells a different story: the night-time trough is much deeper. At midnight, summer demand sits at around 195.5 GW, while winter drops to 151.9 GW. By early morning, winter is the lowest of the three, but it then climbs fast, a sharp shoulder as heaters and lights come on before dawn.

Yet across all seasons, one pattern holds stubbornly: the evening is always a peak. In summer and monsoon, the evening high blends into a long elevated stretch; in winter, it is a pronounced spike after the day’s work. The hour of the absolute high may slide, summer’s peak is often in the afternoon heat, winter’s right after sunset, but the grid never gets a quiet evening. That persistence is why the timing question matters year-round, not just in May.

## Why does the exact hour matter more every year?

Because the single hardest hour the grid has to serve keeps climbing. India’s all-India peak demand met was about 158.8 GW in 2017. By 2024, it had hit a record 248.7 GW on 30 May at 3pm, a 57% increase in seven years. The 2025 figure, 240.4 GW from a partial year, will almost certainly be surpassed when remaining months are tallied.

Each new record raises the stakes for that evening ramp. When the annual peak was 159 GW, the climb from a midday belly to the evening high was one size. At nearly 250 GW, the same shape demands much more from the generators and wires that must carry that evening surge. The grid can add more solar, sure, but that only deepens the midday belly; it does not touch the seven-o-clock peak. The mismatch between solar’s hours and the hour of highest need grows wider as both total demand and solar capacity increase. That is why the exact hour of peak demand matters at a scale it never did before: the same clock problem becomes more expensive every year.

## How should you read these numbers?

These curves come from Grid-India, the national and regional load despatch centres under the Ministry of Power. The hourly demand, solar generation, and wind data for 2024 were compiled in a Mendeley Data dataset released under a Creative Commons CC-BY licence; the long-run annual peak series is republished by NITI Aayog’s India Climate & Energy Dashboard (ICED). All figures are all-India aggregates and are reported as gigawatts (GW).

A few honest boundaries. The hourly numbers measure “demand met”, electricity actually supplied. If any demand went unserved because of load shedding or grid constraints, that is not in these figures, so they represent a floor on true demand. The daily shape you see for a season is a “typical day,” an average over all the days in that season; no single real date will match the smooth curve exactly. The “demand net of solar” line is simply total demand minus solar generation at each hour. It is the load left for hydro, wind, gas, nuclear, and coal together, not the output of any one fuel. And because these are national totals, they smooth over very different regional grids: states with heavy solar penetration, like those in the west and south, can show a much deeper duck curve than the all-India average implies.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The shape of net electricity demand across a day when a lot of solar power is on the grid. It dips low in the middle of the day (the belly) and rises steeply in the evening (the neck), like a duck's profile. It shows how solar reduces midday load but leaves the evening peak untouched.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's grid now shows this shape because solar pushes net demand down at midday, but the real peak arrives after sunset.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Total electricity demand minus the power generated by solar at that moment. It is the load that all other power sources—coal, gas, hydro, wind, nuclear—together must supply. It does not represent any single fuel's output.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The duck curve is about net demand, not total demand. It reveals the timing problem left for non-solar generators.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A unit of power equal to one billion watts. Think of it as the rate of electricity use; 1 GW can power roughly 700,000 typical Indian homes at once.

glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Our data is demand met, so it is a floor on true demand. The actual peak demand could be higher if the grid had no constraints.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: An average day constructed by taking the mean of all days in a season. No single date looks exactly like this smooth curve, but it represents the general underlying pattern.

chartExplainers.title: Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks after dark
chartExplainers.takeaway: On an average summer day, net demand sags to about 161 GW at 1pm but then climbs to roughly 202 GW by 7pm, after solar has vanished—a 40 GW ramp in six hours.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows three lines for a typical summer day in 2024: total electricity demand met, solar generation, and net demand (demand minus solar). Total demand runs high, around 210 GW through the late morning and afternoon. Solar generation rises from near zero at 6am to a peak of about 48 GW around midday, covering about 22% of total demand at 1pm. Subtract solar and net demand dips to a low of about 161 GW. As the sun goes down, solar output drops toward zero by 6pm. Meanwhile, demand stays elevated into the evening, pushing net demand up sharply to around 202 GW by 7pm. The net demand curve—low belly, steep neck—is the duck curve. It reveals that solar provides huge midday relief but does nothing for the evening peak, leaving a large and fast ramp for the rest of the power fleet to meet.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the gap between total demand and net demand—that is solar's contribution. It is wide at noon and gone by evening. The net demand line is what non-solar sources must cover.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume net demand equals coal or any single fuel; it represents the combined load for all generators other than solar. Also, this is a seasonal average, not a specific date.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The three lines can be displayed with thick strokes and clear labels to stay readable on small screens, with touch targets for time values.

chartExplainers.title: How the daily peak moves with the season
chartExplainers.takeaway: Winter demand plunges much lower overnight—151.9 GW at midnight versus 195.5 GW in summer—but the evening remains a stubborn peak across all seasons.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart plots average demand met for three seasons in 2024: summer (March-May), monsoon (June-September), and winter (October-February). Summer and monsoon demand are high and plateau-like from late morning into the evening, staying above 190 GW for many hours. Winter demand traces a deeper trough in the small hours, dropping to around 145 GW by 3am, and then rises sharply through a morning shoulder to peak in the early evening. Despite these shifts, the early evening—roughly 6pm to 8pm—emerges as a peak point in all three curves. The absolute timing can slide: on some days the record high is in the afternoon, but the early evening consistently sees demand near or at its daily maximum. This seasonal persistence of the evening peak means that the timing mismatch with solar is not just a summer story; it is built into the year-round rhythm.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the lines at midnight to see the deep winter dip; then follow each line to the evening to see how they all converge toward a high point.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume winter demand is low overall. The dip is only in the small hours; the morning and evening peaks are still substantial.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a multi-line chart with distinct colors and an hour-by-hour slider or thumbnail view to make comparison easy on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: India's peak demand keeps breaking records
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's all-India peak demand met rose from 158.8 GW in 2017 to a record 248.7 GW in 2024—a 57% increase in seven years—making the evening ramp harder each year.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the single highest instantaneous demand met in each year from 2017 to 2025. The climb is steep and steady: 158.8 GW in 2017, 173.9 GW in 2018, 182.4 GW in 2019, 180.9 GW in 2020 (a slight dip during the pandemic year), then resuming upward to 199.7 GW in 2021, 209.9 GW in 2022, 237.4 GW in 2023, and 248.7 GW in 2024—set on 30 May at 3pm. The 2025 point, 240.4 GW from a partial year, is already close and will almost certainly be exceeded. Each new annual peak raises the grid’s requirement for the hour of maximum strain. When that peak falls in the afternoon (as in 2024), it does not erase the evening high—net demand still ramps steeply post-sunset. As the annual record pushes toward 250 GW and beyond, the duck curve’s evening neck demands ever more generation and storage that can respond quickly.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each point is a year's single highest demand met, in GW. The upward trend is clear. Note that the 2024 record came at 3pm, but the annual peak can shift from afternoon to evening across years.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are single-hour peaks, not average demand. An afternoon annual peak does not mean the evening ramp has eased; the daily duck shape remains.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a simple line with large dots for each year and a minimal y-axis to keep the trend crisp on small screens.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India's electricity demand peaks in the evening around 7pm, after solar generation has fallen to near zero, creating a steep ramp in the grid's net load that no amount of midday solar can cover.
requiredConcepts: The spine of the article and the meaning of the duck: on an average summer day (March to May, 2024) India's electricity demand runs around 210 GW through the late morning and afternoon, while solar generation peaks at about 48 GW around midday. Subtract solar from demand and the residual 'net demand' sags to a midday belly of about 161 GW around 1pm, then climbs steeply to an evening peak of about 202 GW around 7pm. That evening climb is roughly a 40 GW rise in about six hours. The shape of that net-demand line, low belly then sharp evening neck, is what grid operators call the duck curve.

The single most important number: solar covers about 22% of demand at 1pm but essentially 0% at the 7-8pm peak, because the sun has set exactly when demand is highest. This is why simply building more solar does little for the hardest hour: more panels deepen the midday belly but add nothing to the evening peak.

The honest framing of 'demand net of solar': it is an arithmetic residual, demand minus solar generation, and it represents the load that everything other than solar must meet (hydro, wind, gas, nuclear and coal together), NOT the amount of coal burned. Do not say coal fills the gap by name; say it is the load left for the rest of the fleet, and that the steep evening ramp is what flexible generation and storage have to cover.

The seasonal point, from 2024 typical days: the daily shape moves with the season. In summer and the monsoon, demand stays high from late morning into the evening; in winter the night-time trough is deeper and the morning shoulder is sharper, with the day's low coming in the small hours rather than at midday. Across seasons the evening remains a stubborn high point.

Why it matters more every year, the peak-growth context: the all-India peak demand met has risen from about 159 GW in 2017 to a record of about 249 GW in 2024, roughly a 57% increase in seven years (the 2024 record was set on 30 May; the 2025 figure, about 240 GW, reflects a partial year at the time of compilation).

VINTAGE AND SCOPE DISCIPLINE: the intraday curves are averages over the 2024 calendar year, a snapshot of today's grid and not a multi-year trend; the annual-peak series runs 2017 onward. 'Demand met' excludes any demand that was shed or went unserved, so it is a floor on true demand. Every figure is an all-India aggregate; regional grids differ, and the article must not imply one national curve describes every state.

NUMBER DISCIPLINE is absolute: every statistic must come from the evidence packet's locked numbers or the specific figures stated in these concepts; never invent, recall or estimate. Present figures as rounded approximations ('about 48 GW', 'roughly 202 GW around 7pm', 'about 57% higher'), never false-precision decimals. Anchor every number to what it measures when it first appears, and always give power in gigawatts (GW).

Keep the macha layer warm and plain-spoken, a sharp friend explaining why the grid's new headache is a clock problem, not a size problem: India got very good at asking how much power it needs, and solar is real and growing fast, but the sun clocks off at exactly the wrong time, so the evening is where the strain now lives. The playfulness lives in the headings; the body stays grounded and genuinely useful, and the closing summarises what the whole page means, not one chart.

plannedCharts.title: Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks after dark
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The whole storage argument in one chart: solar slashes midday demand, but the day's peak lands in the evening, when solar has gone to zero.

plannedCharts.title: How the daily peak moves with the season
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The peak is not fixed to one hour: it travels across the day as the seasons turn.

plannedCharts.title: India's peak demand keeps breaking records
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Why the shape matters more every year: the single hour the grid has to serve keeps climbing.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
